newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Zaire "high-risk" for business now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Zaire "high-risk" for business now.

text.p: With rebels pressing an advance, the United States on Monday renewed pressure on Americans to leave Zaire, saying the country is too high a security risk.
"And so our message is clear as a bell to the American private community. Get out of Zaire. Get out of Zaire before you find yourself in harm's way," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"There are missionaries there who believe, obviously, that they are doing necessary work. There are business people there who are chasing profits, chasing contracts, and obviously they and their companies have decided it's worth the risk," he told reporters.
But he said: "We think it's a high risk, frankly."
"Business people, NGOs (non-government organisations), missionaries, the situation is too precarious, too unstable for them to stay," he added.
He spoke after the United States had again reduced its official diplomatic presence in the capital of Kinshasa from to 25 from 37.
Despite repeated earlier appeals, Burns said some 325 private Americans were still in the country but "we are not in a position to force American citizens to leave Zaire."

He said one factor in U.S.-decision making was a flurry of rumours over the weekend that Zaire's government was prepared to kill foreigners in order to draw foreign intervention forces into the civil war that the government is losing.
"Now we don't believe that rumour was true, but we have a responsibility to take it seriously, and so we have taken some very significant security precautions over the weekend," Burns said.
He described the situation as most uncertain, including with the Zairean army, now in its barracks in Kinshasa.
The army "doesn't have a great track record about civil law and order in the past, and we are mindful of that," he said.

Burns said the United States would keep its embassy open as long as possible because an American presence is important during the current "endgame" and when the transition of power in Zaire takes place.
The forces of rebel leader Laurent Kabila renounced a pledge to halt their advance on Kinshasa and continued their advance on the capital.

South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who is trying to avert a bloody battle for Kinshasa, said Wednesday's planned meeting between Kabila and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko on board a South African naval ship could be the last hope for a peaceful settlement. Rebel spokesmen said in Lubumbashi on Monday that Mobutu was running out of time.
